2022_236_final_2022_2023_soc_recommendat.paragraph: Presentation slides and an accompanying February 15, 2022 memo from Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent for Elementary Instruction, and Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent for Secondary Instruction, setting Troy School District's Schools of Choice (SOC) participation level for the 2022-2023 school year. Drawing on Plante Moran Cresa enrollment projections, current SOC enrollment data, and a sibling survey emailed to existing SOC families, the administrators recommend accepting SOC applications for 18 Kindergarten, 3 First Grade and 16 Middle School students, with middle school students placed in a building according to available space. Supporting data show 285 elementary SOC students against 4,847 non-SOC students in 2021-2022, a 5.55% SOC share.
2022_236_final_2022_2023_soc_recommendat.page:
Purpose and Presenters
Recommendations for Schools of Choice, 2022-2023 School Year, prepared by Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent, Secondary Instruction, and Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction. Schools of Choice provides non-resident students with additional enrollment opportunities; participation is optional for districts, and the degree and extent of participation - including application enrollment dates, grade levels, and building assignment - are determined at the local level.

Subgroups: EL 56 SOC (19.65%) vs 1,324 non-SOC (27.32%); Free/Reduced Lunch 44 (15.44%) vs 527 (10.87%); Special Ed 24 (8.42%) vs 407 (8.40%).

Non-SOC Enrollment by Grade, 2021-2022

Sibling Preference Survey
A survey was emailed to current SOC families about siblings eligible for Kindergarten, 1st Grade, and 6th-8th Grade in 2022-2023: 18 Kindergarten students plan to attend, 3 First Grade students, and 16 middle school students (6th, 7th and 8th combined).

Recommendations
Use Plante Moran Cresa enrollment projection numbers as the foundation for determining SOC admissions for 2022-2023, and accept SOC applications for 18 Kindergarten, 3 First Grade and 16 Middle School students. The memo anticipates many more than 18 kindergarten applicants, allowing 18 to be admitted initially with the option of admitting more, if space allows, in the third week of August. Middle school students would be placed in a building according to available space. The memo also carries forward earlier boilerplate describing the 2016-2017 recommendation, which referenced Fred Ignatovich's 1.5 enrollment projection formula (most likely + low/2), acceptance of applications for 100 Kindergarten and 30 First Grade students, limiting SOC kindergarten applicants to the full-day program, and sibling-preference admission to Baker Middle School only.
2022_236_final_2022_2023_soc_recommendat.verbose:
Title and authorship. "Recommendations for Schools of Choice, 2022-2023 School Year," prepared for the Troy School District Board of Education by Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent, Secondary Instruction, and Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction. The closing slide reproduces a memorandum dated February 15, 2022, addressed to the TSD Board of Education from Kris Griffor, Asst. Supt., Elementary Instruction, and Christine DiPilato, Asst. Supt., Secondary Instruction, on the subject "Schools of Choice Recommendations for the 2022-2023 School Year."

Program framing. Schools of Choice provides non-resident students with additional enrollment opportunities. Participation in Schools of Choice is optional for districts, and the degree and extent of participation are determined at the local level, including application enrollment dates, grade levels, and building assignment.

Elementary enrollment projections submitted by Plante Moran Cresa. The slides compare "Most Likely" projections against "Actual" counts for Kindergarten and First Grade. For 2019/2020, Kindergarten most likely 835 versus actual 838, and First Grade most likely 891 versus actual 888. For 2020/2021, Kindergarten most likely 844 versus actual 761 (as of 1/28/21), and First Grade most likely 884 versus actual 829 (as of 1/28/21). For 2021/2022, Kindergarten most likely 845 versus actual 803 (as of 1/27/22), and First Grade most likely 851 versus actual 792 (as of 1/27/22). For 2022/2023 the most likely projections are 807 for Kindergarten and 820 for First Grade, with actuals shown as unknown.

Data summary, elementary SOC versus non-SOC students, 2021-2022 school year, by building. Barnard Elementary 22 SOC and 424 non-SOC, 4.93% SOC, change -3.80%. Bemis Elementary 4 and 461, 0.86%, -0.33%. Costello Elementary 32 and 387, 7.64%, -2.68%. Hamilton Elementary 27 and 423, 6.00%, -1.34%. Hill Elementary 71 and 289, 19.72%, 1.08%. Leonard Elementary 25 and 372, 6.30%, -2.05%. Martell Elementary 16 and 357, 4.29%, -1.14%. Morse Elementary 7 and 402, 1.71%, 0.09%. Schroeder Elementary 1 and 437, 0.23%, 0.02%. Troy Union Elementary 11 and 409, 2.62%, -0.96%. TSD Preschool 0 and 80, 0.00%, 0.00%. VLAC 0 and 49, 0.00%, change NA. Wass Elementary 46 and 376, 10.90%, -0.07%. Wattles Elementary 23 and 381, 5.69%, 2.40%. Hill Elementary carries by far the highest SOC concentration among the elementary buildings.

By grade level. TSD preK 0 SOC and 80 non-SOC, 0.00% SOC, 0.00% change. Kindergarten 39 SOC and 684 non-SOC, 5.39%, 1.69%. First 48 and 744, 6.06%, 0.64%. Second 39 and 781, 4.76%, -0.21%. Third 41 and 816, 4.78%, 0.16%. Fourth 41 and 867, 4.52%, -3.84%. Fifth 77 and 875, 8.09%, -1.76%. The total is 285 SOC students and 4,847 non-SOC students, 5.55% SOC, with a change of -0.69%.

Ethnicity breakdown. Among SOC students: Asian 45 (15.79%, change -5.68%); Black 20 (7.02%, 1.19%); Hawaiian/Pacific Islander 1 (0.35%, -0.26%); Hispanic 12 (4.21%, 0.22%); Multi-ethnic 22 (7.72%, 2.20%); Native American 0 (0.00%, 0.00%); White 185 (64.91%, 2.33%); total 285 at 100.00%. Among non-SOC students: Asian 1,936 (39.94%, change -1.85%); Black 225 (4.64%, 0.74%); Hawaiian/Pacific Islander 8 (0.17%, -0.12%); Hispanic 239 (4.93%, 0.50%); Multi-ethnic 240 (4.95%, 0.97%); Native American 1 (0.02%, -0.02%); White 2,198 (45.35%, -0.23%); total 4,847 at 100.00%. The SOC population is majority White while the non-SOC population is split more evenly between White and Asian students.

Subgroup breakdown. English Learners: 56 SOC students, 19.65% of SOC, change 3.39%; 1,324 non-SOC students, 27.32%, change 1.08%. Free/Reduced Lunch: 44 SOC, 15.44%, change -2.96%; 527 non-SOC, 10.87%, change -2.03%. Special Education: 24 SOC, 8.42%, change 0.75%; 407 non-SOC, 8.40%, change -0.19%.

Non-Schools of Choice enrollment by grade, 2021-2022. Kindergarten 764 (asterisked as including PreK/Dev Kdg), 1st 744, 2nd 781, 3rd 816, 4th 867, 5th 875, 6th 861, 7th 830, 8th 912, 9th 966, 10th 971, 11th 972, 12th 991, for a total of 11,350.

Kindergarten and First Grade enrollment history. 2009-2010: 739 and 817. 2010-2011: 752 and 785. 2011-2012: 727 and 832. 2012-2013: 768 and 795. 2013-2014: 766 and 814. 2014-2015: 700 and 787. 2015-2016: 755 and 728. 2016-2017: 798 and 769. 2017-2018: 812 and 845. 2018-2019: 800 and 871. 2019-2020: 792 and 845. 2020-2021: 734 (asterisked) and 785. 2021-2022: 764 (asterisked) and 744. The asterisk denotes that the figure includes PreK (Developmental Kindergarten).

Projected sibling preference placement. A survey was emailed to current Schools of Choice families requesting information on siblings who would be eligible for Kindergarten, 1st Grade, and 6th, 7th and 8th Grade for the 2022-2023 school year. The number of Kindergarten students that plan to attend is 18; the number of 1st Grade students is 3; and the number of middle school students (6th, 7th and 8th combined) is 16.

Factors considered. The memo lists the factors weighed in framing the recommendation: current enrollment across the Troy School District; enrollment projections, patterns and trends; numbers and percentages of Schools of Choice students currently in the district; the projected number of Schools of Choice siblings who would be age-eligible to enter the district in 2022-2023 if the decision is made to admit a "Limited" number of kindergarten, first, and sixth through eighth grade students under Schools of Choice; and available elementary classrooms.

Recommendations for 2022-2023. The administration recommends that the district use Plante Moran Cresa enrollment projection numbers as the foundation for determining the number of Schools of Choice students to admit for the 2022-2023 school year, and accept SOC applications for 18 Kindergarten, 3 First Grade and 16 Middle School students. Based on the number of kindergarten applications received for 2022-2023, the administration anticipates attracting many more than 18 applicants, which would allow the district to admit 18 kindergarteners initially with the option of admitting additional students, if space allows, in the third week of August. Middle school students would be placed in a building according to available space.

Carried-over prior-year language. The memo slide also retains text describing the recommendation for the 2016-2017 school year, listing the same categories of factors and recommending that the district use Fred Ignatovich's 1.5 enrollment projection numbers with his recommended formula (most likely + low/2) as the foundation for determining SOC admissions; noting that "actual" enrollment as of the February Count for both kindergarten and first grade was above both Ignatovich's "Most Likely" and "Low" 2015-16 projections; recommending acceptance of SOC applications for 100 Kindergarten and 30 First Grade students, with the expectation of more than 100 kindergarten applicants based on 2015-2016 volume and the option to admit additional students in the third week of August; limiting Schools of Choice kindergarten applicants to the full-day kindergarten program; and accepting "Sibling Preference" applications only for siblings of current SOC students, to attend Baker Middle School only, where enrollment for the following year was estimated at approximately 728 and accepting 15 applications during the initial application process was said to bring the district extremely close to an ideal total student population at Baker while allowing more admissions in August if space permitted.

2022_237_m011822org_regbdmtg.paragraph: Minutes of the Troy Board of Education organizational and regular meeting held January 18, 2022 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. The Board re-elected Karl Schmidt president, Dr. Wilson vice president, and Gary Hauff secretary, each through December 31, 2022, and adopted the annual housekeeping resolutions on treasurer, depositories, legal counsel, meeting schedule, and committee assignments, all by 7-0 votes. On the business side the Board awarded site work for the retention pond project to Simone Construction Services for $416,176.50 from the Building and Site Sinking Fund. The meeting adjourned at 8:22 p.m.
2022_237_m011822org_regbdmtg.page:
Meeting and Attendance
Board meeting minutes for January 18, 2022, held at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. Present in addition to Mr. Schmidt were Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, and Wilson; also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Godfrey, and West. Approximately 14 members of the audience attended. Mr. Schmidt explained that the evening's meeting is where the Board elects officers, appoints committee members for the upcoming year, and approves or authorizes items considered on an annual basis, with the regular meeting following the organizational portion.

Organizational Actions (all votes 7-0)
| Item | Action |
|---|---|
| 22-001 | Mr. Schmidt to serve as acting chairperson until election of a president (moved Philippart, supported Wilson) |
| - | Judy Holmes appointed temporary secretary |
| 22-002 | Mr. Schmidt elected president until December 31, 2022; roll call 7-0 |
| 22-003 | Dr. Wilson elected vice president until December 31, 2022; roll call 7-0 |
| 22-004 | Mr. Hauff elected secretary until December 31, 2022; roll call 7-0 |
| 22-005 | Rick L. West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, appointed Treasurer for January through December 2022 |
| 22-006 | Resolution on Fund Depositories and Investments adopted for January through December 2022 |
| 22-007 | Legal counsel designations continued for calendar year 2022 |
| 22-008 | Superintendent continued as Deputy Secretary of the Board for 2022 |
| 22-009 | Judy Holmes designated to post notices of meetings for 2022 |
| 22-010 | 2022 calendar-year meeting schedule adopted |
| 22-011 | Board Committee Memberships for 2022 adopted |

Depositories and Legal Counsel
Depository institutions named: Bank of America, Citizens Bank, JP Morgan Chase Bank, Comerica Bank, Huntington Bank, Fifth Third Bank, Flagstar Bancorp, MILAF (Michigan Liquid Asset Fund Plus, managed by PFM Asset Management, Inc. through Fifth Third Bank), and PNC Bank. Funds may be invested according to Board Policy 5000.06, and the Treasurer may combine money from more than one fund under subsection (1)(h) of Section 380.1223 of the Revised School Code. Designated legal counsel: Clark Hill, PLC; Collins & Blaha, P.C.; Miller Johnson; Thrun Law Firm, P.C.; and Miller Canfield.

Recognition
Seniors Lucia Lee (Athens) and Heejin Shyn (Troy High) were honored for Japanese speech contest awards, along with teacher Mina Mori. January was recognized as School Board Appreciation Month, tied to the district's World Class for ALL - Project 26 strategic plan.

Consent Agenda (22-012)
Approved items A, B and C: minutes of the December 7, 2021 Board Workshop; minutes of the December 14, 2021 Board Meeting; and the Treasurer's Report for November 2021. Vote 7-0. Student representatives Alyssa McLarty (Troy College and Career High School), Yara Mashal (International Academy-East), Sasha Palmkoeck (Athens High School), and Sarayu Bethamcherla (Troy High School) reported on school events.

Business
22-013 awarded the bid for flooring replacement work, approved as an expenditure of the Capital Projects Fund and/or Building Site and Sinking Fund (7-0). 22-014 awarded the bid for site work projects to Simone Construction Services in the amount of $416,176.50, approved as an expenditure of the Building and Site Sinking Fund (7-0).

Public Comment and Closing
Six residents spoke, most on the student mask mandate, the "Test to Stay" program, and diversity instruction. Board members discussed high school graduation venues, weighing Pine Knob against the O'Rena and a Tuesday evening versus a Saturday. The next Board Workshop was set for Tuesday, February 1 at 6:00 p.m. and the next regular meeting for Tuesday, February 15 at 7:00 p.m., both at the Services Building. The meeting adjourned at 8:22 p.m.; minutes submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary.
2022_237_m011822org_regbdmtg.verbose:
Meeting identification. Board of Education, Troy, Michigan. Board meeting minutes for January 18, 2022, held at the Troy School District Services Building, located at 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, present were Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, and Wilson. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Godfrey, and West. There were approximately 14 members of the audience. Mr. Schmidt explained that this evening's meeting is where the Board elects officers, appoints committee members for the upcoming year, and approves or authorizes items that must be considered on an annual basis, and that the regular Board meeting would follow the organizational portion of the meeting.

Election of acting chairperson (22-001). It was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Dr. Wilson that Mr. Schmidt serve as acting chairperson to officiate the meeting until the election of a president has been completed. Yes 7, No 0.

Appointment of temporary secretary. Mr. Schmidt appointed Judy Holmes to act as temporary secretary until such time as the secretary of the Troy Board of Education has been elected.

Nomination and election of president (22-002). Acting Chairperson Schmidt declared nominations in order for the office of Board president. Dr. Philippart nominated Mr. Schmidt. It was moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mr. Hauff that nominations be closed; Yes 7, No 0. It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mr. Hauff that Mr. Schmidt serve as president of the Troy Board of Education until December 31, 2022. Roll call vote: Philippart yes, Schmidt yes, Wilson yes, Anne yes, Gottlieb yes, Hammond yes, Hauff yes. Yes 7, No 0.

Nomination and election of vice president (22-003). President Schmidt declared nominations in order. Mr. Hauff nominated Dr. Wilson. It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Dr. Philippart that nominations be closed; Yes 7, No 0. It was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Anne that Dr. Wilson serve as vice president until December 31, 2022. Roll call vote: Schmidt yes, Wilson yes, Anne yes, Gottlieb yes, Hammond yes, Hauff yes, Philippart yes. Yes 7, No 0.

Nomination and election of secretary (22-004). President Schmidt declared nominations in order. Dr. Wilson nominated Mr. Hauff. It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mrs. Hammond that nominations be closed; Yes 7, No 0. It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mrs. Hammond that Mr. Hauff serve as secretary until December 31, 2022. Roll call vote: Wilson yes, Anne yes, Gottlieb yes, Hammond yes, Hauff yes, Philippart yes, Schmidt yes. Yes 7, No 0.

Appointment of school board treasurer (22-005). It was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mr. Gottlieb that Rick L. West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, be appointed as Treasurer of the Troy Board of Education for the period January through December 2022. Yes 7, No 0.

Establish fund depositories and investments (22-006). Moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mr. Gottlieb that the Board adopt the resolution on Fund Depositories and Investments for the period January through December 2022, with a copy of the attached resolution incorporated in its entirety as part of the official minutes. The resolution recites that public monies, including tax monies, may come into the hands of Rick West, Treasurer of Troy School District, and that under Michigan law the Board must provide by resolution for the deposit of all such monies in one or more banks. The Treasurer is directed to deposit and/or invest all public monies in his name as Treasurer into the following depository institutions: Bank of America, Citizens Bank, JP Morgan Chase Bank, Comerica Bank, Huntington Bank, Fifth Third Bank, Flagstar Bancorp, MILAF (Michigan Liquid Asset Fund Plus, managed by PFM Asset Management, Inc. through Fifth Third Bank), and PNC Bank. Monies may be withdrawn by checks signed with a facsimile signature of Treasurer Rick West, and in emergencies by the handwritten signature of Rick West or Superintendent Richard M. Machesky, who may sign on the General Fund account and the Payroll account at Bank of America. Accounts established at PNC Bank for paying Troy Career Center expenses may be drawn on by checks with the handwritten signature of the Troy Career Center Manager, Assistant Manager, or Program Coordinators. The Treasurer may open or close accounts with the listed institutions provided it is in the interest of the District. Funds may be invested according to Board Policy 5000.06, and the Treasurer is authorized to combine money from more than one fund for the purpose of making an investment authorized by subsection (1)(h) of Section 380.1223 of the Revised School Code; the maximum amount to be invested with the above institutions is regulated by the school code. The certification reads: "I, Gary Hauff, Secretary of Troy School District, Oakland County, Michigan, certify that the Resolution was adopted by said Board at a meeting thereof held on the date specified above," given under hand and seal this 18th day of January 2022. Yes 7, No 0.

Designation of board and district legal counsel (22-007). Moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Dr. Philippart to continue the designation of Clark Hill, PLC; Collins & Blaha, P.C.; Miller Johnson; Thrun Law Firm, P.C.; and Miller Canfield as legal counsel to advise and/or represent the Troy School District and Board of Education as necessary for the 2022 calendar year. The superintendent is authorized to consult additional counsel as needed with prior notification to the board. Yes 7, No 0.

Designation of superintendent as deputy secretary (22-008). Moved by Mrs. Hammond and supported by Mr. Gottlieb to continue the designation of the Superintendent of Schools as Deputy Secretary of the Board with authority to act for the secretary for the 2022 calendar year. Yes 7, No 0.

Designation of person for posting notices of meetings (22-009). Moved by Mr. Gottlieb and supported by Mrs. Hammond that the person designated for posting notices of meetings for the 2022 calendar year shall be Judy Holmes, Secretary to the Superintendent of Schools. Yes 7, No 0.

Meeting schedule and committee assignments (22-010, 22-011). Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mr. Hauff that the Board adopt the schedule of meetings for the 2022 calendar year as indicated on the attached calendar; Yes 7, No 0. Moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mrs. Hammond that the Board adopt the Board Committee Memberships for the 2022 school year as attached; Yes 7, No 0.

Recognition - TSD Mission Moment, Japanese Program. The Board recognized two seniors, Lucia Lee from Athens and Heejin Shyn from Troy High, for recent awards in Japanese speech contests. Heejin won the Silver Award in the J.LIVE Talk Japanese Speech Contest hosted by George Washington University in November 2021, one of only three high school students in the nation selected to participate. Lucia Lee took first place in the Michigan Japanese Speech Contest the previous February and was selected by the government of Japan as one of the American High School Ambassadors invited to visit Japan under the Kakehashi Project - The Bridge to Tomorrow Program, spending 10-14 days in Japan the following spring, all expenses paid. Their teacher, Mina Mori, was recognized for advocacy and dedication in expanding the Japanese program in both high schools. The Board congratulated the students and Ms. Mori and presented them with certificates of recognition.

Board Recognition Month. Each January the Troy School District honors and celebrates the trustees of its Board of Education. School Board Appreciation Month recognizes the role Board members play in reinforcing the district mission of ensuring learning for all through policies, fiscal stewardship, and support of world-class teaching and learning. The remarks noted the many hours of preparation, learning, and advocacy devoted to the volunteer position, the importance of teamwork, and the Board's role in the District's Strategic Planning under the banner World Class for ALL - Project 26.

Additions and deletions; first public communication period. None recorded for either.

Consent agenda (22-012). Moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mr. Gottlieb that the Board approve items A, B and C on the consent agenda: minutes of the December 7, 2021 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the December 14, 2021 Board of Education Meeting; and the Treasurer's Report for November 2021. Yes 7, No 0.

Student representatives. Mr. Schmidt invited the student representatives to speak before continuing the meeting since they needed to prepare for mid-terms. Alyssa McLarty reported for Troy College and Career High School, Yara Mashal for International Academy-East, Sasha Palmkoeck for Athens High School, and Sarayu Bethamcherla for Troy High School, each on events and activities in their schools.

Personnel and Curriculum. No items recorded.

Business - Flooring Replacement and Polishing Project (22-013). Moved by Mrs. Hammond and supported by Mrs. Anne that the bid for flooring replacement work be awarded as stated and that the amount be approved as an expenditure of the Capital Projects Fund and/or Building Site and Sinking Fund. Yes 7, No 0. The minutes text does not carry the award amount or vendor name.

Business - Site Work, Retention Pond Project (22-014). Moved by Mr. Gottlieb and supported by Mrs. Hammond that the bid for site work projects be awarded to Simone Construction Services in the amount of $416,176.50 and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the Building and Site Sinking Fund. Yes 7, No 0.

Public communication (non-agenda items). Mr. B. J. Lennon, Troy resident and parent of students in the district, addressed the Board regarding his opposition to the mask mandate in place for students. Mrs. Kacy Bailey, Troy resident and parent, thanked the Board and district for ending the quarantine for close contacts with the "Test to Stay" program and also spoke about her opposition to the student mask mandate. Mr. Ollie Apahidean, Troy resident and parent, read an article written by a Troy resident 10 years earlier about how the Troy Board of Education was at that time. Mr. John Tyson, Troy resident, addressed the Board about the type of diversity being taught in the Troy School District. Mrs. Sarah Krieger, Troy resident and parent of one student in the district, addressed the Board about her opposition to the mask mandate and said she had pulled two of her three students from the district. Mrs. Kelly Jones, Troy resident and parent, expressed gratitude for the recent MLK Day presentation and the district's initiative on diversity, equity, and inclusion and thanked the Board for the work being done for the children.

Board comments. Dr. Philippart thanked Mr. Schmidt, Dr. Wilson, and Mr. Hauff for continuing to serve as officers. Mrs. Hammond asked for a broader discussion on the year's plans for high school graduation ceremonies before a decision is made, and Mr. Schmidt indicated the Board could discuss after comments from Board members. Mrs. Anne also thanked the current officers for remaining another year. Mr. Hauff congratulated the Troy Mindstormers Lego team on qualifying for the FIST Lego League World Championship. Dr. Wilson thanked the pillar captains for their update on the District's Strategic Plan. Dr. Machesky spoke about the MLK Day Celebration and thanked Thomas Butcher and Cornelius Godfrey for their work putting the program together, and again recognized the Board for its dedication and teamwork.

Graduation venue discussion. Mr. Schmidt opened a discussion on high school graduations and asked board members to share their thoughts on venue options. Board members shared concerns about the cost of Pine Knob versus the O'Rena, as well as the ceremony being held on a Tuesday evening rather than a Saturday. Mrs. DiPilato indicated she would be meeting with the high school administration to consider the options and would come to a decision that week.

Upcoming meetings and adjournment. Mr. Schmidt announced that the next Board Workshop would be held Tuesday, February 1st at 6:00 p.m. at the Services Building and the next regular meeting Tuesday, February 15th at 7:00 p.m. at the Services Building. The meeting was adjourned at 8:22 p.m. Minutes respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the typist notation GNH/jh.

2022_238_re_action_alert_help_us_support.paragraph: An email chain forwarded to the Troy Board of Education packet concerning the IDEA Full Funding Act. The K-12 Alliance of Michigan, through Oakland Schools, asked member districts to pass board resolutions supporting the IDEA Full Funding Act of 2021 (HR 5984) ahead of a March 10 trip to Washington, D.C., noting that Congress committed in 1975 to fund up to 40 percent of the additional cost of special education but that the federal investment is today less than 14 percent. Superintendent Richard Machesky forwarded the alert to Board President Karl Schmidt on February 7, 2022, recommending the item be discussed Thursday and placed on the February agenda; Schmidt replied "okiedokie."
2022_238_re_action_alert_help_us_support.page:
Chain of Correspondence
A three-message email thread. The top message is from Karl Schmidt (Troy Board of Education President) to Richard Machesky, copying Judy Holmes, sent Monday, February 7, 2022 at 4:36:01 PM, reading simply "okiedokie." It responds to a forward from Superintendent Richard M. Machesky, Ed.D. (rmachesky2@troy.k12.mi.us, office phone 248-823-4003), sent Monday, February 7, 2022 at 12:28 PM, which stated: "I would also recommend we discuss this on Thursday and prepare to have it on our February agenda." The underlying alert came from the OCSA listserv (ocsa-request@lists.oakland.k12.mi.us) on behalf of Nicole Christian, sent Thursday, February 3, 2022 at 4:57 PM to the OCSA ListServ, copying OSCabinet, David Randels, and Lisa Hansknecht, and forwarded on behalf of David Randels of Oakland Schools.

The Ask
K-12 Alliance members will meet with members of Congress in Washington, D.C. in March to push for full funding of the federal Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), and the alert seeks evidence of broad Michigan support. Districts are asked to work with their school boards to pass resolutions in support of the IDEA Full Funding Act; a sample school board resolution (Sample School Board Resolution.docx) was provided, with the request that boards pass it or a similar resolution at their next meeting if at all possible.

Funding Background
When Congress enacted IDEA in 1975 to ensure all students with disabilities have access to quality public education, it committed to fund up to 40 percent of the additional cost schools would face to provide those services. Today the federal investment in IDEA is less than 14 percent. The IDEA Full Funding Act of 2021 (HR 5984) would require yearly increases to funding for IDEA programs so that the federal government reaches an annual appropriation of 40% of the cost of special education services within the next 10 years.

The Alliance will compile the passed board resolutions and bring them to Washington on March 10th to share with members of Congress. Signatories are Robert McCann, Executive Director, and Katie Whitman-Herzer, Administrative Director, The K-12 Alliance of Michigan, P.O. Box 16085, Lansing, Michigan 48901, United States.

Substance of the appeal. Addressed to "K-12 Alliance Members," the alert states that in March, members from the K-12 Alliance will be meeting with members of Congress in Washington, DC to push for full funding for the federal Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), and that the Alliance needs help demonstrating the broad support behind this effort in Michigan. It recounts that when Congress enacted IDEA in 1975 to ensure all students with disabilities have access to quality public education, Congress committed to fund up to 40 percent of the additional cost schools would face to provide those services. Today, the alert states, the federal investment in IDEA is less than 14 percent, and "it's long-past time for that to change."

The legislation. The IDEA Full Funding Act of 2021, identified as HR 5984, would require yearly increases to funding for IDEA programs so that the federal government reaches an annual appropriation of 40% of the cost of special education services within the next 10 years, described as finally fulfilling the obligation made back in 1975.

Requested action. While the Alliance works with Michigan's Congressional delegation, it asks recipients to work with their school boards to pass resolutions in support of the IDEA Full Funding Act. The Alliance created a sample resolution, referenced as the attachment "Sample School Board Resolution.docx," and asks that boards pass it or a similar resolution at their next meeting if at all possible. The stated goal is to go to Washington in March with resolutions from as many districts as possible, both to show the level of support for the action and to convey the meaningful change it would make in schools going forward.

Submission logistics. Passed resolutions can be shared with Katie Whitman-Herzer by emailing her at katie@k12michigan.org. The Alliance will compile and bring all of the passed board resolutions to Washington on March 10th and share them with members of Congress. The message is signed by Robert McCann, Executive Director, and Katie Whitman-Herzer, Administrative Director.
